report.releaseDate: Sep 2026 data: Kansas Lottery sports-wagering & lottery reports (early/mid Oct 2026); KRGC casino revenue reports (c. 14–19 Oct 2026)
report.currency: USD (tables in $ millions unless stated; Kansas reports in USD so no FX conversion required)
report.verdict: September 2026 confirms Kansas as a small, mature, structurally low-yield regulated market: sportsbook handle fell for a third straight YoY reading (-5.9% to $267.0m) while a still-thin 4.58% hold lifted taxable net revenue 48.7% to $12.2m and the state's 10% cut to just $1.2m — under half a cent per dollar wagered. Land-based GGR grew 3.8% to $34.4m and lottery sales 6% to $46.5m on iLottery, but the real story is regulatory: the 2025 contract-renewal moratorium has lapsed, Boot Hill/DraftKings have already locked in to 2030, and the 2027 session is the last window for legislators who want a larger take before all remaining sportsbook contracts expire on 31 Aug 2027.

summary: **Three verticals, two regulators, one owner.** Kansas gaming is constitutionally 'owned and operated' by the Kansas Lottery under the Kansas Expanded Lottery Act (KELA, 2007) and SB 84 (2022), with the Kansas Racing and Gaming Commission (KRGC) as the regulator/enforcer for the four state-owned casinos, sports wagering, the Gilley's historical-horse-racing (HHR) hall and parimutuel racing. Four federally recognised tribes run compact casinos whose revenue is not published.

**September 2026 sports handle $267.0m, -5.9% YoY** (Sep-25: $283.7m) — the third consecutive YoY decline, per the Kansas Lottery monthly report as relayed by Gaming Intelligence and RG.org. MoM the NFL restart lifted handle +64.7% from August's $162.1m.

**Net (taxable) sports revenue $12.2m, +48.7% YoY**, but only because hold recovered from a near-record-low 2.90% in Sep-25 to 4.58%; 2026 football-adjacent months have held 3.90%, 7.32%, 4.05% and 4.58% — three of four under 5% versus the 8–10% normal in mature US states. Kansas 'revenue' is net of winnings, promotional/free-play deductions, the 0.25% federal excise and carry-over, so it is a NGR-type base, not GGR.

**State take is structurally tiny.** The 10% state share on net revenue produced $1.22m in September (0.46% of handle). FY2025 (Jul-24–Jun-25): ~$2.7bn handle, $172.8m sports-wagering revenue, ~$17m retained by the state (0.6% of handle); year one (Sep-22–Aug-23) delivered just $7m on $1.85bn of bets. Legislators flagged this in Sept 2025 hearings as the core grievance.

**Online is >97% of sports handle.** Sep-25 split: online $277.6m / retail $6.1m (97.8%/2.2%); Jul-26: online $165.6m / retail $1.7m (99.0%/1.0%), with retail revenue just $0.2m. Retail handle fell 38.6% YoY in Mar-26. The Sep-26 channel split was not in the sources we could open — n/a.

**A DraftKings-led duopoly with a real third tier.** DraftKings held 44.7% of online handle in Jul-26 ($74.0m; $4.6m net rev) vs FanDuel 28.9% ($47.8m; $4.1m) and bet365 9.1% ($15.1m); no other brand exceeded $1.1m revenue. In Mar-26 DK/FD were 36.0%/29.5% with 'others' 34.5% — more fragmented than most small states. Seven brands live: DraftKings (Boot Hill), FanDuel & bet365 (Kansas Star), theScore Bet (Hollywood; replaced ESPN BET), BetMGM, Caesars, Fanatics (Kansas Crossing).

**Land-based GGR $34.4m in September, +3.8% YoY** (KRGC via CDC Gaming): slots $30.5m (+3.1%, 89% of GGR), tables $3.9m (+10%). Hollywood Casino at Kansas Speedway $14.5m (+4.9%), Kansas Star $13.0m (flat), Boot Hill $3.7m (+11.2%), Kansas Crossing $3.2m (+4.5%). 9M-2026 total ~$325m; CY2025 casino GGR implied ~$427m from the 3% local share of $12.8m (AGA).

**Casino tax is high and tiered: 27% or 29% of GGR** (22%/24% state + 3% host local governments + 2% Problem Gambling and Addictions Grant Fund), fixed in 15-year management contracts. Implied September take at 27% ≈ $9.3m (estimate). AGA puts total 2025 Kansas gaming tax revenue at $135.3m across casinos and sports.

**HHR is the new land-based growth engine.** Phil Ruffin's Gilley's Gambling Hall (Park City/Wichita; ~1,000 HHR machines, authorised by SB 84 for a single Sedgwick County facility) opened 15 Dec 2025 and recorded $29.4m of HHR handle and 59,396 patrons in Jan-26, $26.3m in Apr-26, $28.2m in May-26 and $184.2m fiscal-YTD by May. The state share is 3% of amount wagered ($0.88m in Jan-26). KRGC reports these as unaudited parimutuel figures outside the casino total; Sep-26 figure n/a.

**Lottery sales $46.5m in September, +6% YoY, led by iLottery** (eInstants/eDraw via the PlayOn app and playonkansas.com); July 2026 sales were +51% YoY on the same driver (Gaming Intelligence headlines; product mix behind the paywall). Lottery play is 18+, sports wagering 21+.

**Licensing is contract-based, not open.** SB 84 lets each of the four lottery gaming facility managers run retail sportsbooks plus up to three interactive platforms (max 12 skins statewide; 7 used), up to 50 retail partner locations each (incl. Kansas Speedway), and an extra skin via a pro team (Sporting KC). The Lottery owns the product; managers and platforms keep 90% of net revenue; the state 10%, of which 80% is earmarked for the Attracting Professional Sports to Kansas Fund.

**The 2025 moratorium has lapsed — and the first renewal is done.** SB 125 (2025 budget, veto by Gov. Kelly overridden) barred the Lottery from negotiating or extending any sports-wagering management contract through FY2026 (to 30 Jun 2026). In Aug 2026 the Lottery granted Boot Hill (Butler National) a three-year extension to 2030 and DraftKings extended its Boot Hill deal 10 years on 'updated commercial terms'. The other three casinos' 5-year contracts still expire 31 Aug 2027.

**Political direction: more take, not more product.** Sept 2025 legislative hearings explored raising the 10% rate, differentiating online/retail rates, curbing promo deductions and even a single-source model; operators and casinos opposed. The 2026 session produced no iGaming bill and no sports-wagering tax change that we could verify — the 2027 session (Jan–May 2027) is the decisive window before the Aug-2027 expiries.

**Tribal expansion is the other competitive front.** Three of four tribes (Prairie Band Potawatomi, Iowa Tribe, Sac & Fox) have compact amendments for on-reservation sports wagering; Gov. Kelly and the Wyandotte Nation signed a new Class III compact on 31 Mar 2026 covering the 7th Street Casino (KCK) and Crosswinds Casino (Park City), now in federal review, with Crosswinds slated to grow from ~800 to ~1,400 slots plus a 238-room hotel by summer 2027 — directly against Kansas Star and Gilley's in the Wichita catchment.

**Missouri is eroding the Kansas City arbitrage.** Kansas' per-capita handle was inflated by Missouri residents crossing into Kansas; Missouri's own online launch (1 Dec 2025) coincides with Kansas' run of YoY handle declines (-4.3% Jun-26, -5.9% Sep-26). Untaxed prediction markets are a second leakage channel operators have openly cited.

**Payments and RG are standard US-online, lightly specified in statute.** Deposits run through the usual debit/ACH/e-wallet/prepaid stack; we could not verify a statutory credit-card prohibition [unverified]. The 2% casino levy funds problem-gambling treatment (~$8.5m in 2025), KRGC administers voluntary self-exclusion, and SB 84 delegated sports-advertising rules to the Lottery rather than codifying content limits.

**Read-through for B2Tech:** Kansas is not an entry market for a new B2C sportsbook — skins are controlled by four casino managers, five are unused, promo intensity is extreme and the base is shrinking. The accessible angles are B2B (platform/HHR/iLottery content and trading services to incumbents), a skin deal with a casino whose contract is being re-papered before Aug-2027, or positioning for any 2027 re-tender if legislators force a model change.

**Data quality:** September 2026 headline figures are corroborated across at least two outlets relaying the Kansas Lottery/KRGC reports, but the underlying PDFs could not be opened in this cycle; operator-level and channel splits for September, Gilley's September handle and lottery product mix are n/a.

segments.name: Sports betting (online & retail)
segments.headline: Shrinking handle, promo-depressed hold and a 10% rate on an NGR-type base make Kansas the lowest-yield sportsbook state per dollar wagered — yet the Boot Hill/DraftKings extension shows incumbents still value the footprint.
narrative: The Kansas Lottery's September 2026 report, relayed by Gaming Intelligence and RG.org, shows settled wagers of $267,020,698 across the seven online brands and four retail books, down 5.9% from $283,742,310 in September 2025 and the third consecutive year-on-year decline. The month-on-month jump of roughly 65% from August's $162.1m is purely the NFL and college-football calendar. Taxable revenue was $12,216,725, up 48.7% from $8,215,618, but that comparison flatters: September 2025's 2.90% hold was among the thinnest ever recorded by a US state in a football month, and 4.58% this year remains far below the 8–10% that mature markets like New York or Illinois run. Of the four most recent months, only July (7.32%) cleared 5%; June was 3.90% and August 4.05%. Because Kansas defines 'sports wagering revenue' net of winnings, promotional and free-play deductions, the 0.25% federal excise and negative carry-over, the figure is closer to NGR than GGR, and the state's 10% share — $1,221,673 in September — equates to 0.46% of handle.

Channel mix is almost entirely digital. In September 2025 online handle was $277.6m against $6.1m retail (97.8%/2.2%) and in July 2026 the split was $165.6m against $1.7m (99.0%/1.0%), with retail producing only $196,639 of the month's $12.24m net revenue. Retail handle collapsed 38.6% YoY in March 2026 to $4.13m, of which Hollywood Casino (theScore Bet) took $1.59m and Kansas Star (FanDuel) $1.36m. The September 2026 channel split was not available in the material we could open and is shown as n/a. The practical implication is that retail sportsbooks exist as regulatory anchors for skins rather than as profit centres; an operator's Kansas P&L is an online P&L.

Market structure is a DraftKings-led duopoly with an unusually thick tail. In July 2026 DraftKings processed $73.96m of online handle (44.7%) and $4.60m of net revenue, FanDuel $47.79m (28.9%) and $4.07m, and bet365 — a 2025/26 entrant via Kansas Star — $15.1m; no other brand exceeded $1.1m of revenue. In March 2026 the leaders held 36.0% and 29.5% respectively with 'others' at 34.5%, and in September 2025 DraftKings' $118.4m handle (42.7% of online) generated only $1.9m of revenue versus FanDuel's $4.2m on $89m — evidence that DraftKings has bought share with promotions that are deductible from the tax base. The seven live brands are DraftKings (Boot Hill), FanDuel and bet365 (Kansas Star), theScore Bet (Hollywood, replacing ESPN BET after Penn's late-2025 brand exit), and BetMGM, Caesars and Fanatics (all via Kansas Crossing). Five of the twelve statutory skins are unused, but each is gated by a casino manager's commercial decision and Lottery approval.

Fiscal-year data from the Kansas Lottery's budget submissions and the Legislative Research Department put FY2025 sports-wagering revenue at $172.8m on roughly $2.7bn of handle, with managers and platforms retaining about $157.3m (the 90%) and the state about $17m — 0.6% of handle. The Lottery's own FY2026 and FY2027 budget lines for the managers' 90% ($108.0m and $139.5m) imply total net revenue of roughly $120m and $155m respectively, i.e. the state itself expected FY2026 to be a down year. In the first twelve months after the 1 September 2022 launch, Kansans and visitors staked $1.85bn for a state return of $7m. RG.org's framing — 'a promotional arms race was supposed to buy growth; Kansas is paying for one and shrinking anyway' — is harsh but numerically fair.

Competitive leakage explains the handle trend better than demand fatigue. Kansas' per-capita handle has long been inflated by Missouri residents in the Kansas City metro crossing the state line; Missouri's own online market launched on 1 December 2025, and Kansas handle has printed YoY declines since (June -4.3%, September -5.9%). Operators have also pointed to untaxed, federally regulated sports prediction markets as an alternative they could pivot to — a lever DraftKings had in hand while negotiating its Boot Hill extension. For an operator, Kansas handle of roughly $2.3–2.6bn a year at a 5–7% blended hold is a $130–170m net-revenue pool shared seven ways, with the top two taking ~70%.

On product and content, all major US sports plus college (including in-state teams), motor racing and KRGC-approved special events are permitted at 21+, with up to 50 retail kiosk partners per casino and a reserved pro-team skin for Sporting Kansas City that has not been activated in any report we saw. The Lottery, not KRGC, writes advertising rules under SB 84. The Boot Hill–DraftKings 10-year amendment 'on updated commercial terms' is the template to watch: the three remaining casino managers must re-paper their Lottery contracts before 31 August 2027, and any change in revenue share, skin fees or promo-deduction treatment will surface there first.

segments.name: Land-based casinos & historical horse racing
segments.headline: Four state-owned casinos grind out low-single-digit growth at a 27–29% tax; the step-change is Gilley's 1,000-machine HHR hall and the coming tribal build-out around Wichita.
narrative: KRGC's September 2026 revenue reports show combined GGR of $34.4m for the four lottery gaming facilities, up 3.8% year on year but down 6.3% from August's $36.7m, with electronic gaming machines contributing $30.5m (+3.1%) and table games $3.9m (+10%). Hollywood Casino at Kansas Speedway (Penn Entertainment, Northeast zone) led with $14.5m (+4.9%; slots $13.1m, tables $1.4m), Kansas Star (Boyd Gaming, Mulvane, South Central zone) was flat at $13.0m with slots down 2.1% to $11.1m and tables up 20.4% to $1.9m, Boot Hill (Butler National, Dodge City, Southwest zone) rose 11.2% to $3.7m and Kansas Crossing (Pittsburg, Southeast zone) 4.5% to $3.2m. Gaming Intelligence puts the nine-month 2026 total at close to $325m, consistent with a ~$430m calendar year; the AGA's disclosure that host local governments received $12.8m (their 3% share) in 2025 implies CY2025 GGR of about $427m, so 2026 is tracking roughly flat to +1%.

The fiscal architecture is fixed by KELA and the 15-year management contracts: managers remit 27% or 29% of GGR depending on contractual revenue thresholds — 22% or 24% to the state's Expanded Lottery Act Revenues Fund, 3% to the host city and county and 2% to the Problem Gambling and Addictions Grant Fund (about $8.5m in 2025). On September's $34.4m that implies roughly $9.3m of gaming tax at the lower tier (our estimate). Each zone is limited to a single casino, so there is no greenfield casino licence available in Kansas; entry is only by acquiring a manager (as Boyd did with Kansas Star) or via the tribal route. The AGA counts $722.1m of 2025 commercial gaming revenue for the state including sports betting and $135.3m of gaming tax across both verticals [AGA figures as parsed from its State of the States 2026 Kansas page; not independently re-verified].

The material change in the land-based landscape is Gilley's Gambling Hall in Park City on the former Wichita Greyhound Park site, opened 15 December 2025 by Phil Ruffin under the SB 84 authorisation for up to 1,000 historical horse racing machines at a single Sedgwick County facility. KRGC's agenda packets record HHR handle of $29.45m and 59,396 patrons in January 2026, $26.29m in April, $28.15m in May and $184.2m fiscal-year-to-date by May, with a state share of 3% of the amount wagered ($0.88m in January, $2.08m FYTD by January). KRGC reports these as 'unaudited parimutuel facility revenue' and excludes them from the casino total; CDC Gaming's January headline of 'statewide revenue up 105%' simply adds the HHR handle to casino GGR and should not be read as like-for-like. Gilley's draws from the same Wichita catchment as Kansas Star, whose slot revenue has softened (April GGR -4.5%, September slots -2.1%). The September 2026 Gilley's figure was not available (n/a).

Tribal supply is also rising. The Prairie Band Potawatomi (Prairie Band Casino & Resort, Mayetta), Kickapoo, Sac & Fox and Iowa Tribe casinos operate under compacts with no public revenue reporting; three tribes have amended compacts to permit on-reservation sports wagering. On 31 March 2026 Governor Kelly and the Wyandotte Nation signed a new Class III compact covering the 7th Street Casino in Kansas City, Kansas and Crosswinds Casino near Park City, cleared by the House 99–20 and now in federal review; the Crosswinds plan adds a 238-room hotel and lifts the floor from ~800 to ~1,400 machines with completion targeted for summer 2027. That puts a second large competitor into the Wichita market within 18 months of Gilley's opening. Separately, KRGC is re-licensing live racing at Eureka Downs (occupational licence applications from 5 October 2026), the first live horse racing in Kansas in years and a modest parimutuel/simulcast adjacency.

For an operator or supplier, the commercial implications are twofold. Land-based margins in Kansas are compressed by the 27–29% levy and the Lottery's ownership model, so the value is in supply (EGM content, HHR systems — Konami and Ainsworth HHR products were approved by KRGC in 2025 — systems and sportsbook kiosks) rather than operation. And the Wichita market is about to be over-supplied relative to its population, which is why Boyd's Kansas Star has been investing in a hotel and leaning on its FanDuel/bet365 skins to defend share.

segments.name: Lottery & iLottery
segments.headline: iLottery is now the growth driver of a ~$45–50m-a-month lottery, and the Lottery's dual role as operator and owner of all expanded gaming gives it unusual leverage over the whole market.
narrative: Gaming Intelligence reports Kansas Lottery sales of $46.5m for September 2026, up 6% year on year and led by iLottery, following a 51% year-on-year jump in July 2026 on the same driver; the detailed product mix (instants, Powerball/Mega Millions, Keno, eInstants) sits behind the paywall and the Lottery's own monthly 'Traditional Lottery' and 'iLottery' revenue PDFs could not be opened in this cycle, so we show product-level figures as n/a. Lottery sales are turnover, not GGR, and are not additive to casino GGR or sports net revenue. The Lottery sells through its PlayOn loyalty platform and the playonkansas.com/app storefront, which now carries eInstant and eDraw games alongside retail scratch, pull-tab, Fast Play and draw games; the minimum age is 18 versus 21 for sports wagering.

Institutionally the Kansas Lottery is more than a lottery. Its FY2027 budget narrative describes two businesses — 'Traditional Lottery' and 'Expanded Lottery', the latter being ownership of the state's casino games and sports wagering and administration of the facility-manager contracts. Its FY2026 budget shows casino gaming revenues of $401.4m flowing through its accounts against $309.5m of related expenditures, and sports-wagering payouts to managers of $102.6m (FY2024), $157.3m (FY2025), $108.0m (FY2026 est.) and $139.5m (FY2027 est.). In other words, the Lottery's own forecasts anticipated a 30% fall in FY2026 sports net revenue versus FY2025, then a partial rebound.

The iLottery ramp matters for an operator for two reasons. First, it demonstrates Kansas regulators' willingness to put real-money digital instant games in consumers' hands at 18+ while the legislature has shown no appetite for commercial iGaming (no online casino bill was introduced in the 2026 session). The state-run eInstant channel is therefore the only legal digital casino-style product in Kansas and will be defended as a Lottery franchise. Second, the Lottery's growing digital competence and player database make it a more credible counterparty in any future 'single-source' or Lottery-run sportsbook model, which legislators floated in 2025 as an alternative to renewing the private skins — the DC/Oregon-style model the Sports Betting Alliance warned about. Suppliers of iLottery content and platform services are the natural beneficiaries of the current trajectory.

segments.name: Licensing, contracts & tax
segments.headline: A closed, contract-based regime: four casino managers control all commercial gaming and skins, tax is fixed by contract and statute, and the Aug-2027 contract cliff is the only open door — which the Lottery has started closing on incumbents' terms.
narrative: Kansas' constitution permits only a state-owned and operated lottery, so KELA (2007) made the Lottery the legal owner of casino gaming in four exclusive zones — Northeast (Hollywood at Kansas Speedway), South Central (Kansas Star), Southwest (Boot Hill) and Southeast (Kansas Crossing) — each run by a private 'lottery gaming facility manager' under a 15-year contract with a one-off privilege fee and a 22–24% state share plus 3% local and 2% problem-gambling levies. SB 84 (effective 1 July 2022) bolted sports wagering onto the same chassis: the Lottery offers sports wagering 'through' the managers, each of whom may run an in-person book, up to 50 retail partner locations and up to three interactive platforms under Lottery-approved marketing agreements; a fourth skin is reserved for a professional-team partnership (Sporting KC). The managers and their platforms retain 90% of net revenue; the state keeps 10%, of which 80% is dedicated to the Attracting Professional Sports to Kansas Fund (the Chiefs-relocation war chest), with smaller statutory carve-outs for problem gambling and white-collar crime enforcement [carve-out detail per our reading of SB 84 summaries; not re-verified this cycle]. KRGC licenses and audits managers, platforms, suppliers and key employees; the Lottery writes the advertising and contract rules.

There is no licence an outside operator can apply for. Access is by (i) acquiring a facility manager, (ii) signing a skin agreement with one of the four managers, subject to Lottery approval, or (iii) a tribal partnership under an amended compact. Platform-level fees are set in the private marketing agreements, not in statute; the KRGC's published fee schedule covers background and licence costs for managers, platforms, suppliers and employees but not a market-access fee [schedule not opened this cycle — n/a]. Operators pay the 0.25% federal excise on handle, which is deductible from the Kansas base, and the 10% state share on net revenue.

The contract cliff is the live regulatory issue. All original sports-wagering management contracts were five-year agreements expiring 31 August 2027. The 2025 appropriations act (SB 125) carried a proviso — vetoed by Governor Kelly and overridden by the Republican supermajority on 11 April 2025 — barring the Lottery from spending anything to negotiate, extend or renew those contracts in FY2025–26, i.e. until 30 June 2026. Hearings in September 2025 made the legislative intent explicit: with the state netting about $17m on $2.7bn of FY2025 handle, members wanted a higher rate, differentiated online/retail rates, limits on promo deductions and consideration of a single-source model; operators and casinos opposed any change to the model. Once the proviso lapsed, the Lottery moved quickly: in August 2026 it granted Boot Hill's manager BHCMC (Butler National) a three-year extension to 2030 on 'the same material terms', and DraftKings and Boot Hill amended their arrangement for ten years on 'updated commercial conditions'. We found no evidence that the 2026 session changed the 10% rate, the promo-deduction rule or the skin cap, nor that it renewed the proviso.

Our reading of the direction of travel: the Lottery and the casino managers have the procedural initiative and will try to re-paper Kansas Star, Hollywood and Kansas Crossing before the 2027 session gets traction, which would leave legislators the blunter tools of a tax-rate amendment or a renewed spending proviso. A rate increase to 15–20% on the existing net base, or disallowance of promo deductions at 10%, are the two most probable outcomes if the legislature acts; a wholesale single-source conversion is a tail risk given the contracts now in place. For an incoming operator, the asymmetry is clear — the only time Kansas market access is genuinely negotiable is between now and August 2027, and the counterparty is a casino manager, not the state.

segments.name: Competition, payments, responsible gambling & political direction
segments.headline: Missouri, prediction markets and tribal expansion are compressing the Kansas opportunity from outside while legislators try to compress operator margins from inside; RG and payments rules are standard-US and not the binding constraint.
narrative: The single largest exogenous shock to Kansas sports wagering is Missouri. Until December 2025 Kansas was the only legal online market in the Kansas City metro, and a disproportionate share of its $2.7–3.0bn annual handle came from Missourians crossing into Wyandotte and Johnson counties; Missouri's statewide online launch on 1 December 2025 removed that arbitrage and Kansas has posted year-on-year handle declines in every month we could observe since (June -4.3%, September -5.9%). The second leakage channel is federally regulated sports event contracts (prediction markets), which carry no state tax or gaming-law obligations; DraftKings' ability to 'walk away and launch sports markets' was explicitly noted as leverage in its Boot Hill renegotiation. Neither is within the Kansas legislature's control, which is why its instinct has been to extract more from what remains.

On the supply side, land-based competition is intensifying around Wichita (Gilley's HHR since December 2025; Crosswinds tribal expansion to ~1,400 slots by summer 2027) and in Kansas City, Kansas (the Wyandotte 7th Street Casino moving to Class III). Hollywood at Kansas Speedway, the largest property, also faces Missouri's riverboat casinos across the state line. The four state-owned properties' combined GGR of roughly $430m a year has been essentially flat since 2023, and the new supply is more likely to redistribute than grow it.

Payments in Kansas follow the standard US online stack — debit cards, ACH/online banking, PayPal and similar e-wallets, Play+ prepaid cards and cash-at-retail services — with retail lottery dominated by cash and the Lottery's PlayOn app handling digital purchases. We could not verify from a primary source whether Kansas statute or Lottery rule bars credit-card funding of sportsbook accounts [unverified]; it is not among the states with a well-publicised ban. There is no mobile-money dimension and no payment-related friction that would differentiate Kansas from neighbouring states.

Responsible-gambling architecture is funded rather than prescriptive. The 2% levy on casino GGR (about $8.5m in 2025) and a slice of the sports-wagering state share feed the Problem Gambling and Addictions Grant Fund; the Kansas Coalition on Problem Gambling runs the 800-522-4700 helpline; KRGC administers a voluntary exclusion programme covering the state-owned casinos and sportsbooks; minimum ages are 21 for sports wagering and 18 for lottery and HHR. SB 84 directed the Lottery to adopt rules on sports-wagering advertising, management contracts, integrity and licensing rather than codifying content restrictions; we are not aware of Kansas-specific whistle-to-whistle, college-campus or bonus-advertising bans beyond the operators' national AGA code commitments [regulatory text not re-read this cycle]. College betting, including on in-state teams, is permitted.

Politically, the market is in a trust deficit with its legislature. The supermajority's willingness to override the governor on the SB 125 proviso, the September 2025 hearings on taxing 'less than 1%' of $2.7bn, and the fact that 80% of the state's sports take is ring-fenced for luring the Chiefs rather than general revenue all point to a 2027 session that will be transactional. Operators' best defence is the one they are already deploying — long-dated, Lottery-approved contract extensions that raise the political cost of a model change — plus the argument that Missouri competition, not the tax rate, is what is shrinking the base. For B2Tech, the watch-item is whether any 2027 bill reopens skin allocation (e.g. untethering platforms from casinos or adding a Lottery-run skin); that, not a tax tweak, would be the event that creates entry optionality.

highlights.text: Contract re-papering window is open now: with the SB 125 moratorium lapsed on 30 Jun 2026 and Boot Hill/DraftKings already extended to 2030, Kansas Star, Hollywood and Kansas Crossing must re-sign before 31 Aug 2027 — the only moment skin economics and five unused skins (of 12) are genuinely negotiable.

Hold normalisation is pure upside to net revenue: September's 4.58% is still roughly half the mature-market norm; every 1pt of hold on ~$2.5bn annual handle is ~$25m of net revenue, 90% retained by operators under the 10% regime.

Lowest-tier tax burden for operators: 10% on an NGR-type base with uncapped promo deductions and deductible federal excise leaves 90% of net revenue with managers/platforms — the most operator-friendly fiscal terms in the Midwest while they last.

iLottery and HHR show digital/machine-based products are growing where sports is not: lottery sales +6% (Sep-26) and +51% (Jul-26) on eInstants; Gilley's ~$26–29m of monthly HHR handle in year one — real B2B demand for content, HHR systems and platform services.

Supply-side M&A optionality in land-based: entry to Kansas casino gaming is only via acquiring a facility manager (Boyd's Kansas Star precedent) or a tribal partnership — the Wyandotte Class III compact and Crosswinds expansion create a new partner set in 2027.

Fragmented tail: 'other' brands took 34.5% of online handle in Mar-26 and bet365 reached 9% within months of launch, showing a Kansas skin can still win share from the duopoly with product and pricing rather than promo spend.

lowlights.text: Base erosion from Missouri: Kansas handle has declined YoY in every month observed since Missouri's 1 Dec 2025 launch (-4.3% Jun-26, -5.9% Sep-26) and the KC-metro cross-border premium that made Kansas punch above its 2.9m population is gone for good.

Legislative appetite for a bigger take: Sept-25 hearings targeted the 10% rate, promo deductions and even a single-source model; a supermajority that overrode the governor once can raise the rate or renew the proviso in the 2027 session before the Aug-2027 expiries.

Promo-driven hold volatility: three of the last four months held under 5% (3.90%, 7.32%, 4.05%, 4.58%) and DraftKings earned $1.9m on $118m of handle in Sep-25 — a market where share is bought with deductible free bets is hostile to a late entrant's unit economics.

Closed access and casino gatekeepers: no licence exists to apply for; skins are allocated by four casino managers under Lottery approval, retail is <2% of handle and economically irrelevant, and there is no iGaming pathway (no bill in 2026).

Wichita over-supply: Gilley's 1,000 HHR machines (since Dec-25) plus Crosswinds' expansion to ~1,400 slots and a 238-room hotel (summer 2027) will redistribute a flat ~$430m land-based GGR pool; Kansas Star is already flat with slots -2.1%.

Earmarking distorts politics: 80% of the state's sports take funds the Attracting Professional Sports to Kansas Fund, so the general fund sees almost nothing — weakening the fiscal constituency for the current model and strengthening the case for change.

Transparency gaps: the Lottery's detailed monthly PDFs and KRGC packets could not be opened this cycle; Sep-26 channel/operator splits, Gilley's September handle and lottery product mix are unverified or n/a.

forecast.intro: The regulatory bridge from the 2025 status quo to 2027 runs through three dates: 30 Jun 2026 (SB 125 renewal moratorium expired — done), Jan–May 2027 (legislative session; last chance to change the 10% rate, promo deductions or the skin model before contracts roll), and 31 Aug 2027 (expiry of the original five-year sports-wagering management contracts for Kansas Star, Hollywood and Kansas Crossing; Boot Hill already extended to 2030). Commercially, the Kansas Lottery's own budget implies FY2026 sports net revenue fell ~30% to ~$120m before recovering toward ~$155m in FY2027, driven by hold rather than handle.

forecast.view: Our independent view: Kansas sports handle falls a further **5–10% in FY2027 to roughly $2.3–2.5bn (estimate)** as Missouri's market matures, while blended hold drifts up to **5.5–6.5%** as promo spend rationalises, leaving net revenue of **~$130–150m (estimate)** — in line with the Lottery's $139.5m manager-retention budget — and a state share of ~$13–15m unless the rate changes. We assign a **~55–60% probability that the 2027 session raises the sports-wagering rate (most likely to 15–20%) and/or caps promo deductions**, a ~25% probability of no change, and a ~15% tail of a renewed proviso or single-source conversion; the Lottery's pre-emptive extensions make the tail less likely each month. Land-based GGR stays **flat to +1% (~$430–435m CY2026 estimate)** with Gilley's adding **~$300–340m of annual HHR handle (estimate)** outside that total and the Wichita market turning share-redistributive in 2027. iLottery keeps lottery sales growing mid-single digits; **commercial iGaming is not on the table before 2028**. Market leverage is low (state-owned assets, no debt-funded licence fees), so the swing factors are purely regulatory and competitive.
watch: 2027 Kansas legislative session (Jan–May 2027): any bill amending K.S.A. 74-8700 et seq. on the 10% rate, promo deductions, online/retail differentiation, skin allocation or a Lottery-run book; and whether the FY2028 appropriations bill revives the SB 125 proviso.

Kansas Lottery contract actions: extensions for Kansas Star (Boyd/FanDuel/bet365), Hollywood (Penn/theScore Bet) and Kansas Crossing (BetMGM/Caesars/Fanatics) ahead of 31 Aug 2027, and whether any of the five unused skins or the Sporting KC skin is activated.

Monthly Kansas Lottery sports reports: online/retail split, hold trajectory (sustaining >5% in Q4-26 NFL months) and the DraftKings-vs-FanDuel revenue gap as a proxy for promo intensity; cumulative YoY handle vs Missouri's reported KC-metro handle.

KRGC: Gilley's monthly HHR handle and patron counts, Kansas Star slot trend, Eureka Downs racing licence, and federal (DOI) approval timing for the Wyandotte compact and the Crosswinds expansion (target summer 2027).
Prediction-market encroachment: CFTC/court rulings on sports event contracts and any Kansas AG or KRGC action, which affects both the handle base and operators' negotiating leverage.
Kansas Lottery iLottery monthly revenue reports and any legislative attention to eInstants as de facto online casino — the leading indicator for a future iGaming debate.
